about: Questions John has said the site must answer. Each one is tested by probes: multiple-choice questions a newcomer should be able to answer from the site. A probe with evidence is answered on the built site, and CI checks that it stays answered. A probe with no evidence yet is a gap the next goal audit turns into a ticket. See README.md.
not_sure: Not sure / the site doesn't say

questions.asked: how does the UK tax, debt and spending compare to other major nations
questions.reading: Major nations is read as the G7 (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK and the US), with the wider OECD as context. Tax and spending are compared as a share of GDP; debt as general government gross debt as a share of GDP. Bond markets are read as government borrowing costs (10-year government bond yields) and debt interest paid as a share of GDP, compared with the G7. Yields reflect several things (central bank rates, expected inflation, how much is being borrowed and investors' view of risk), so the site should show them and explain what moves them without presenting them as a verdict on any government.

options.B: Higher than all three
options.C: Higher than Germany but lower than France and Italy
options.D: About the same as all three

probes.why: International page, 2024: UK 34.4% of GDP, against France 43.5%, Italy 42.8% and Germany 38.0%.

evidence.text: France 43.5%
Italy 42.8%
Germany 38.0%
United Kingdom 34.4%

questions.asked: Are rish people really not paying enough tax?
questions.source: John, project chat, 2026-11-04 (question 4 of his list of ten)
questions.reading: "Enough" is a value judgment, so the site gives the measured facts and does not say what is enough. The facts are: the share of Income Tax and of all taxes paid by top income groups, the share of income that each fifth of people pays in tax (including National Insurance, VAT and other taxes on spending), how the top rates compare with other countries, and what the main proposals (for example, a wealth tax or aligning Capital Gains Tax with Income Tax) are estimated to raise. Each is shown with its year, population and source.

probes.question: In tax year 2023 to 2024, what share of all Income Tax did the top 1% of Income Tax payers owe?
probes.why: Who pays page: the top 1% of Income Tax payers owed 27.2% of all Income Tax in 2023 to 2024, and had 12.4% of Income Tax payers' income. The 59.1% is the top 10%'s share of Income Tax.

evidence.text: the top 1% of Income Tax payers owed 27.2% of all Income Tax, and had 12.4% of all Income Tax payers' income

probes.question: Across 1999-00 to 2023-24, how did the top 1%'s share of Income Tax compare with their share of income?

options.A: Lower than their share of income in every year
options.B: Equal to their share of income
options.C: Higher than their share of income in every year
options.D: Higher in some years and lower in others

probes.why: Who pays page, Income Tax by person: the top 1%'s share of Income Tax was higher than their share of income in every year from 1999-00 to 2023-24.

evidence.text: The top 1%'s share of Income Tax was higher than their share of income in every year from 1999-00 to 2023-24

probes.question: What does the 46.0% figure for the richest fifth of people in 2023/24 measure?

options.A: The share of their income that they paid in tax
options.B: The share of all taxes paid by UK households that the richest fifth paid
options.C: The tax rate on the top income band
options.D: The share of all government revenue, including borrowing

probes.why: Who pays page: the richest fifth paid 46.0% of all taxes paid by UK households. The page says this is a share of the total, not the share of income that goes on tax (36.2%), and covers household taxes, not all government revenue.

evidence.text: In 2023/24 the richest fifth of people paid 46.0% of all taxes paid by UK households.
A share of the total, not the share of income that goes on tax

probes.question: In 2023/24, how did the share of gross household income that went on all taxes compare between the highest-income fifth and the lowest-income fifth?

options.A: The highest-income fifth paid a much larger share
options.B: The two shares were less than one percentage point apart
options.C: The lowest-income fifth paid a much larger share
options.D: Both paid about a quarter of their income in tax

probes.why: Tax and income page (household-tax.html): taxes took a similar share of income for the lowest-income fifth (36.7%) and the highest-income fifth (36.2%) in 2023/24, less than one percentage point apart.

evidence.text: Taxes took a similar share of income for the lowest-income fifth and the highest-income fifth in 2023/24, less than one percentage point apart

probes.question: In 2023/24, how much of the highest-income fifth's gross household income went on Income Tax alone?
probes.why: Tax and income page: for people in the highest-income fifth most tax is direct, and Income Tax alone was 22.3% of gross household income. The 36.2% is all taxes for that fifth.

evidence.text: Income Tax alone was 22.3% of gross household income

probes.question: According to the site, how much would the main proposals to tax wealth or capital gains more heavily raise each year?

options.A: An official estimate of about £10 billion a year
options.B: The site gives no estimate for those proposals; it does not show what they would raise
options.C: Less than £1 billion a year, from an official estimate
options.D: Nothing: the proposals would raise no money

probes.why: Who pays page, limits: the site does not estimate what a wealth tax or a change to Capital Gains Tax would raise each year.

evidence.text: The site does not estimate what a wealth tax or a change to Capital Gains Tax would raise each year

probes.question: According to the site, how do the UK's rates on top incomes compare with other large countries?
probes.gap: The international page compares total tax as a share of GDP, but does not compare top income tax rates or the tax paid by top earners with other countries.

probes.question: According to the site, what share of all taxes, including VAT and National Insurance, do the top 1% of people pay?

options.A: The site shows the top 1%'s share of all taxes as a percentage
options.B: The site shows the top 1%'s share of Income Tax only, and says it does not show their share of all taxes
options.C: The site shows that the top 1% pay no taxes on spending

questions.asked: Is immigration a good thing or a bad thing?
questions.reading: The site does not say whether immigration is good or bad. That is a judgment that depends on values. It answers what official evidence says about the parts that can be measured: the public-money effects of migrants by type, use of public services, the NHS and care workforce, and population and growth. It says which parts are evidence and which depend on values, and shows the range of credible estimates. Immigration is read as people moving to live in the UK (net migration, all routes), with EU and non-EU migrants shown separately where official figures split them. The answer should be easy to find from the home page in a few taps on a phone.

probes.question: Does the site say whether immigration is a good thing or a bad thing?

options.A: Yes: it is a good thing
options.B: Yes: it is a bad thing
options.C: No: it says the answer depends on what you value, and shows what the evidence says about the measurable parts
options.D: No: it does not discuss the question at all

probes.why: The immigration page opens by saying the site does not answer the question, because the answer depends on what people value, and then sets out the measurable parts.

evidence.text: The site does not answer that question, because the answer depends on what you value.

probes.question: According to official estimates, does a migrant’s effect on public finances depend on their age, visa route or employment?

options.A: No: every migrant has the same effect
options.B: Yes: it depends on things such as visa route, age and employment
options.D: It cannot be estimated at all

probes.why: The MAC estimates the Partner route as a lifetime deficit, and says that partner and Skilled Worker dependants contribute less through taxation than UK residents but are still more fiscally positive. Higher spending as people age and a lower employment rate also change the result.

evidence.text: the partners of British citizens and settled residents, will incur a net lifetime fiscal deficit of -£5.6bn in present value terms
Partner applicants and SW adult dependants can contribute considerably less through taxation than UK residents and still be more fiscally positive.
This, combined with a decline in their employment rate and higher public spending as they age, causes the cohort to incur an annual net fiscal deficit as they remain in the UK.

probes.question: Do official estimates of migrants’ effect on public finances differ between the short run and the long run?

options.A: No: the effect is the same in the short and long run
options.B: Yes: a positive annual contribution in the first two decades, then an annual deficit as they stay in the UK
options.C: Yes: a deficit in the first two decades only

probes.why: The MAC finds a positive annual contribution in a cohort’s first two decades, then a deficit as they stay. The OBR says the fiscal impact is likely to become less beneficial over time.

evidence.text: During their first two decades in the UK, the cohort make an annual positive net fiscal contribution.
The fiscal impacts of migration are likely to become less beneficial over time

probes.question: Does the site show how much migrants use public services such as the NHS, schools and housing, using official figures?
probes.gap: The page says the OBR treats public-service spending as a policy choice, not a fixed link to population. It still needs an official figure for how much migrants actually use public services.

probes.question: In the latest official figures, what share of NHS and adult social care staff in England are non-UK nationals?
probes.gap: NHS and adult social care nationality figures are published as spreadsheet data, and the site has not yet taken them. Both sectors are needed.

probes.question: In the latest ONS population figures, what was the main reason the UK population grew?

options.A: Births were higher than deaths, so natural change was the main reason
options.B: Net international migration was the main reason, and was larger than natural change
options.C: Natural change was the main reason, and net migration was negative

probes.why: ONS mid-year estimates, UK, year to mid-2025: the population grew by 227,700. Net international migration was 222,900 and natural change added 4,900 (652,400 births and 647,500 deaths).

evidence.text: The main reason was net international migration

probes.question: According to official economic estimates, does migration raise GDP per person as much as it raises total GDP?

options.A: Yes, it raises GDP per person by as much as total GDP
options.B: It raises total GDP, but its effect on GDP per person is much more uncertain, and may be slightly positive or slightly negative
options.D: It has no effect on GDP

probes.why: The OBR says net migration has been a significant driver of GDP growth, but its effect on GDP per person is much more uncertain, and was either slightly positive or slightly negative in its scenarios.

evidence.text: Net inward migration has been a significant driver of GDP growth, but its impact on GDP per person is much more uncertain.
the impact on real GDP per person was either slightly positive or slightly negative

probes.question: Where official sources give different estimates of the same thing, does the site show the range rather than one chosen figure?

options.A: No: the site gives one figure for each estimate
options.B: Yes: it shows the range of official estimates and says how uncertain they are
options.C: No: it shows no estimates at all
options.D: Only the government’s own figures are shown

probes.why: The page shows the OBR’s higher and lower migration scenarios, and says they are simplified and highly uncertain, rather than picking one figure.

evidence.text: in which net migration is 200,000 a year higher or lower than in our central forecast.
These scenarios are a simplification and are highly uncertain.
Where official estimates differ, the range is shown.

questions.asked: What are the empirical best ways to get the UK economy into a better position, a ranked list of ten things
questions.reading: Ten options, ranked only by a stated, published, empirical measure, never by the site's opinion. The measure is the size of a published estimate of the effect on the level of GDP (potential GDP) over a stated horizon, shown with its range, cost and uncertainty. Estimates from different sources or models are not like-for-like, so they must not be ranked against each other as if they were; where only one source covers a set of options, the ranking stays inside that set. 'Better position' depends on goals (growth, fairness, the deficit), so the site should say that a second ranking, by cost to the public finances, may differ.

probes.question: According to the OECD's modelling of UK structural reforms, which reform package raises the level of GDP most within ten years?

options.A: Trade barriers and research and development support
options.B: Getting people on long-term sick leave back into work
options.C: Planning reform, full expensing and access to finance
options.D: Keeping the state pension triple lock

probes.why: The OECD estimates planning reform, full expensing and access to finance at +2.1% of potential GDP after 10 years, the largest of its packages (long-term sick +1.4%, trade and R&D +0.5%).

evidence.text: Capital deepening: planning reform, extension of full expensing, access to finance

probes.question: What does the OECD estimate the full combined UK reform package would raise the level of potential GDP by, after ten years and after 25 years?

options.B: +4.0% after 10 years and +7.7% after 25 years

probes.why: The OECD's combined package is +4.0% of potential GDP after 10 years and +7.7% after 25 years.

evidence.text: gives +4.0% of potential GDP after 10 years and +7.7% after 25 years

probes.question: What measure do the OECD's reform estimates use for the size of each effect?

options.B: A percentage of baseline potential GDP

probes.why: The OECD measures each effect as a percentage of baseline potential GDP.

evidence.text: a percentage of baseline potential GDP

questions.asked: Why can't we afford to spend more money on defence
questions.reading: Defence spending is read as the government's official defence spending (PESA, the COFOG defence function), compared with other G7 countries on the same function in OECD figures. "Can't afford" is read as: what would extra spending cost, how could it be paid for, and what would have to give. The premise is contested, so the site sets out the choices and the figures rather than deciding whether the UK can afford more.

probes.question: In 2025-26, how much did the UK government spend on defence, and what share of GDP was that?

options.B: About £65 billion, about 2.1% of GDP

probes.why: PESA 2026 outturn for 2025-26: £65.4 billion, 2.1% of GDP.

evidence.text: In 2025-26 the UK spent £65.4bn on defence, 2.1% of GDP.

probes.question: Compared with 2010-11, was UK defence spending in 2025-26 higher or lower after inflation, and was its share of GDP higher or lower?
probes.gap: The defence comparison now uses the ten-year window the impartiality rule allows (2015-16 to 2025-26), so the page no longer compares with 2010-11, the year this question names. Whether John wants 2010-11 shown as well is a decision for him.

probes.question: In 2024, how did UK defence spending as a share of GDP compare with the other G7 countries that have a figure?

options.B: The second highest, behind the United States

probes.why: OECD Government at a Glance, 2024: UK 2.3% of GDP, behind the United States (3.1%) and ahead of France (1.9%), Germany, Japan and Italy. Canada has no figure in the table.

evidence.text: the second highest of the 6 G7 countries with a figure.
The highest was the United States, at 3.1%.

probes.question: In 2025-26, of every £100 the government spent on services, roughly how much went on defence?
probes.why: PESA 2026: defence was £5.3 of every £100 spent on services in 2025-26; social protection was £33.2 and health £21.0.

evidence.text: defence took £5.3.
Social protection took £33.2 and health £21.0.

probes.question: At 2025-26 levels, about how much would each extra 1% of GDP of defence spending cost in a year?

options.B: About £31 billion

probes.why: 1% of 2025-26 nominal GDP (£3,070 billion, OBR) is £30.7 billion.

evidence.text: Each extra 1% of GDP in defence spending would cost about £30.7bn a year at 2025-26 levels.

probes.question: Which of these does the site set out as ways to pay for extra defence spending?

options.B: Only borrowing
options.C: Borrowing, higher taxes, or spending less on other things

probes.why: The defence page lists three broad ways: borrowing, tax, and less spending elsewhere, and says most plans combine them.

evidence.text: There are three broad ways, and most plans combine them.
Less spending elsewhere.

probes.question: Does the site say whether the UK can afford more defence spending?

options.B: No, it cannot afford more
options.C: It sets out the choices and does not decide
options.D: It says the answer is borrowing

probes.why: The defence page says whether the UK can afford more depends on which costs people accept, and that the page does not decide that.

evidence.text: Whether the UK can afford more depends on which costs people accept, and this page does not decide that for you.

probes.question: How much room do the government's fiscal rules leave for extra defence spending?

options.A: None: the rules are already broken
options.B: About £3 billion a year
options.C: About £15 billion in 2029-30, shared by all spending and tax decisions
options.D: About £31 billion, the cost of one per cent of GDP

probes.why: The OBR's October 2026 central forecast puts the margin against the fiscal mandate at £15 billion in 2029-30, and at £24 billion against the supplementary PSNFL target. That is the room for all extra spending or lower taxes together, not for defence alone.

evidence.text: In the central forecast, the fiscal mandate for the current budget to be in surplus in 2029-30 is met by a margin of £15 billion.
That is the whole budget's room, shared by every decision on spending and tax, not a sum for defence.

probes.question: What does NATO's own figure show for UK defence spending as a share of GDP in 2025?

options.B: About 2.3%

probes.why: NATO's table 3 gives UK core defence spending as 2.32% of real GDP in 2025, a NATO estimate. NATO counts pensions paid to retired military personnel, so its figure is higher than the PESA figure of 2.1% for 2025-26.

evidence.text: In NATO's table, UK core defence spending was 2.28% of GDP in 2024, 2.32% in 2025 and 2.56% in 2026.
NATO counts defence on its own definition, which includes pensions paid to retired military personnel.

questions.asked: did our parents have it easier than this generation?
questions.reading: “Easier” has no single meaning, so the site compares several measures and gives no overall verdict. Parents and this generation are read as people of the same age in two years (for example, people aged 25 to 34 in 1992 and in 2025), not the same people followed through life. The measures are work, buying a home, pay, the cost of university, pensions, tax, school classes, job security and how long people live. Where the site has no figures for a measure at the same age, the probe stays open until the figure is added from an official source.

probes.question: Between April to June 1992 and April to June 2025, how did the share of 25 to 34 year olds in work change?

options.A: It fell by about ten points
options.B: It rose by about ten points
options.D: It rose by about two points

probes.why: Labour Force Survey, UK: 73.6% of 25 to 34 year olds were in work in April to June 1992 and 84.3% in April to June 2025, a rise of about 11 points.

probes.question: Between April to June 1992 and April to June 2025, how did the share of 18 to 24 year olds in work change?

options.A: It rose by about five points
options.B: It fell by about five points
options.D: It fell by about twenty points

probes.why: Labour Force Survey, UK: 65.4% of 18 to 24 year olds were in work in 1992 and 60.7% in 2025. Many in this age group are students.

probes.question: How many times a year’s earnings did the middle-priced home in England and Wales cost in 1999, and in 2025?

options.B: 3.89 times in 1999 and 7.55 times in 2025

probes.why: Ratio of median house price to median full-time earnings, England and Wales: 3.89 in 1999 and 7.55 in 2025. 1999 is the first year measured the same way.

evidence.text: has gone from 3.89 times a year’s earnings to 7.55 times in 2025

probes.question: Between 2008-09 and 2024-25, how did the share of households in England who own their home change? This is all households, not one age group.

options.A: It rose by about three points
options.B: It fell by about three points
options.D: It fell by about ten points

probes.why: English Housing Survey: 67.9% of households owned their home in 2008-09 and 64.8% in 2024-25, a fall of about three points. The figure covers all ages.

evidence.text: Households in England who own their home, all ages 67.9% 64.8%

probes.question: What was the average primary class size in England in January 2006 and in January 2025?

options.B: About 20 in 2006 and about 26 in 2025

probes.why: Average primary class size, England: 26.3 pupils in January 2006 and 26.4 in January 2025, about the same.

evidence.text: Pupils per class 26.3 26.4

probes.question: Were people aged 30 more or less likely to own their home in the 1990s than people aged 30 now?
probes.gap: The site has no home ownership figures by age, so it cannot compare people at 30 with earlier years. Needs English Housing Survey or Labour Force Survey tenure tables by age, from the 1990s.

probes.question: How did pay after inflation for people aged 30 change between 2002 and 2025?
probes.gap: The site has pay figures for all full-time employees, not by age group. Needs median pay by age group from the Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings, with its survey breaks marked.

probes.question: How much did a university degree cost a student in tuition fees and loans in 1998, compared with 2025?

options.A: About the same in both years
options.B: £1,000 in 1998, paid up front; £9,535 in 2025-26 for England

probes.why: House of Commons Library briefing CBP 10155: in 1998 means-tested fees of up to £1,000 across the UK were paid up front rather than through a loan. The cap for home undergraduates in England was announced as £9,535 for 2025-26. The 1998 fee is about £1,934 in 2025 prices (CPIH, calculated).

evidence.text: In 1998 the fee was up to £1,000 across the UK, paid up front rather than through a loan
The 2025-26 figure is the cap for England

probes.question: How has the state pension age changed for people born in 1960 compared with people born in 1990?

options.A: It stayed at 66 for people born in 1960 and 1990
options.B: People born in 1960 reach it at 66 and 0 to 9 months; under current law people born in 1990 reach it at 68
options.D: It rose from 60 to 65 in both years

probes.why: DWP State Pension age timetable: people born in 1960 reach State Pension age at 66 plus 0 to 9 months depending on birth month. For people born from 6 April 1978 it is 68 under current law (Pensions Act 2007, rise from 67 to 68 for 2044 to 2046). A review could change it.

evidence.text: People born in 1960 reach State Pension age at 66 years and 0 to 9 months
For people born from 6 April 1978 it is 68 under current law

probes.question: How long can a 30 year old now expect to live, compared with 30 years ago?
probes.gap: The site has no life expectancy figures by age. Needs ONS national life tables for two or more years, with the age-30 figure.

probes.question: Did a person on the same real income pay more or less tax in 2025 than in 1992?
probes.gap: The site has tax figures by age group for 2023-24 only, and by income band for recent years. Needs income tax and National Insurance on one income level, in each year, from an official source.

probes.question: Has job security changed for people aged 25 to 34 since 1992?
probes.gap: The site has no figures on contract types, temporary work or how long people stay in a job. Needs ONS labour market tables on contracts and job changes by age, from 1992.

questions.asked: Why do we have such high debt in this country?
questions.source: John, project chat, 2026-11-04 (question 1 of 10 in one message)
questions.reading: Why is UK government debt high? Read as public sector net debt (the OBR's measure, net of financial assets, as a share of GDP), its history since 1900, what raised it (borrowing in each year, in particular the 2008 recession, the Covid pandemic and the 2022-23 energy support), and what official bodies say about the causes. The question is about the UK on its own; comparison with other countries is on the borrowing page (J1). Official bodies give more than one view of the causes, so the site shows the figures and the quoted explanations without choosing between them.

probes.question: Since 1900, in which year was UK public sector net debt highest as a share of GDP, according to the site?

options.A: 1918-19, at the end of the First World War
options.B: 1946-47, just after the Second World War

probes.why: Why-debt page, OBR figures: debt was highest in 1946-47, at 249.1% of GDP.

evidence.text: Debt was highest in 1946-47, at 249.1% of GDP.

probes.question: Between 2007-08 and 2009-10, how did UK public sector net debt change, as a share of GDP?

options.A: It fell from about 36% to about 22%
options.B: It stayed at about 36%
options.C: It rose from about 36% to about 65% of GDP
options.D: It rose from about 65% to about 100% of GDP

probes.why: Why-debt page, OBR figures: 35.6% of GDP in 2007-08 and 64.5% in 2009-10.

evidence.text: Debt rose from 35.6% of GDP to 64.5% over the same period.

probes.question: How much did UK public sector borrowing reach as a share of GDP in 2020-21, the first year of the Covid pandemic?

options.B: About 5%

probes.why: Why-debt page, OBR figures: borrowing was 15.0% of GDP in 2020-21.

evidence.text: Borrowing reached 15.0% of GDP in 2020-21

probes.question: According to the ONS, how much did the furlough schemes alone add to borrowing in the year to March 2021?

options.B: £78.2 billion

probes.why: Why-debt page, quoting the ONS (April 2021): the furlough schemes alone added £78.2 billion to borrowing.

evidence.text: with the furlough schemes alone adding £78.2 billion to borrowing in the FYE March 2021.

probes.question: What does the OBR say pushed up borrowing and debt in 2020-21?

options.A: Only the government's own spending decisions
options.B: The impact of the shocks on the economy, combined with the government's response to them

probes.why: Why-debt page, quoting the OBR (July 2025): the impact of the shocks, combined with the government's policy response, pushed up borrowing and debt in 2020-21.

evidence.text: The impact of these shocks on the economy, combined with the Government’s policy response to them, pushed up borrowing to 15 per cent of GDP

probes.question: What is the difference between debt and borrowing, as the site uses the words?

options.B: Debt is what the public sector owes at the end of each year, less its financial assets; borrowing is the amount added during the year
options.C: Borrowing is the total owed; debt is the amount borrowed in one year
options.D: Debt is only the money lent by the Bank of England

probes.why: Why-debt page, opening section: debt is the amount owed at year end, less financial assets; borrowing is the amount borrowed during the year, which adds to debt.

evidence.text: Borrowing is the amount it borrowed during the year, which adds to debt.

probes.question: According to the ONS, what raised interest payable on government debt by £34.0 billion in 2022-23?

options.B: Rises in the Retail Prices Index, which raised the payments on index-linked gilts
options.C: Only the Bank of England's interest rate

probes.why: Why-debt page, quoting the ONS (April 2023): rises in the Retail Prices Index increased the interest payable on index-linked gilts.

evidence.text: as the rises in the Retail Prices Index have increased the interest payable on index-linked gilts.

probes.question: What does the OBR project for the long term, if current policy settings continue?

options.A: Borrowing below 5% and debt below 100% of GDP
options.B: Borrowing above 20% and debt above 270% of GDP by the early 2070s

probes.why: Why-debt page, quoting the OBR (July 2025): on current policy settings, borrowing above 20% and debt above 270% of GDP by the early 2070s, driven partly by an ageing population.

evidence.text: projected to push borrowing above 20 per cent and debt above 270 per cent of GDP by the early 2070s.

questions.asked: Have labour kept their electiion manifesto?
questions.source: John, project chat, 2026-11-04 (question 7 of his list of ten)
questions.reading: Read as whether Labour has kept the pledges in its 2024 manifesto that concern public money and everyday costs: tax, the fiscal rules, defence, housing, the NHS and home energy. Where the wording allows more than one reading (for example "taxes on working people", "basic, higher or additional rates" and the debt measure in the fiscal rules), the site shows each reading and its result, and does not pick one.

probes.question: What did Labour’s 2024 manifesto say it would not increase?

options.A: National Insurance, the basic, higher and additional rates of Income Tax, and VAT
options.B: Council tax, business rates and stamp duty
options.C: Only the basic rate of Income Tax
options.D: Nothing: the manifesto made no tax promises

probes.why: Manifesto, page 21: it will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT. The pledge is about tax on working people.

evidence.text: which is why we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT.

probes.question: Has the government changed the standard VAT rate of 20% since Labour took office?

options.B: Yes, cut to 15%
options.C: No, the standard rate is still 20%

probes.why: The standard rate has stayed at 20%. Budgets changed some reliefs and private school fees, not the standard rate (Full Fact, 28 November 2025).

evidence.text: The standard rate of VAT is still 20%.

probes.question: Have the basic, higher and additional income tax rates on earnings changed since Labour took office?

options.B: Yes, only the additional rate rose

probes.why: The earnings rates are 20%, 40% and 45%, unchanged. The rates on dividends, savings and property income did change (HMRC, Budget 2025).

evidence.text: The basic, higher and additional rates on earnings are still 20%, 40% and 45%

probes.question: What did Budget 2025 do to income tax on dividends, savings and property income?

options.B: Left the rates unchanged
options.C: Raised the rates: dividends from April 2026, savings and property from April 2027

probes.why: HMRC: dividend ordinary and upper rates rise from 6 April 2026; savings and property rates rise from April 2027 (Budget 2025).

evidence.text: Dividend rates rose from April 2026, and savings and property rates rise from April 2027.

probes.question: Why do readers disagree on whether the National Insurance pledge was kept?

options.A: The manifesto does not say whether it covers employer as well as employee contributions
options.B: Labour never mentioned National Insurance in its manifesto
options.C: The rate was cut, which the manifesto ruled out
options.D: The pledge only covered the first year

probes.why: The manifesto mentions National Insurance once. It does not say whether the pledge covers employer contributions, so the government and critics read it differently (Full Fact, 14 October 2024).

evidence.text: It does not say whether the pledge covers employer contributions as well as employee ones

probes.question: Did Budget 2025 extend the freeze on income tax and National Insurance thresholds?

options.A: No, it ended in April 2028 as planned
options.B: Yes, to April 2031

probes.why: Budget 2025 extended the freeze by three years, from April 2028 to April 2031 (Budget 2025 speech; Full Fact, 26 November 2025).

evidence.text: extended the freeze on income tax and National Insurance thresholds for three more years, to April 2031.

probes.question: Did Labour’s private school VAT measure take effect, and when?

options.B: No, it was dropped

probes.why: VAT at the standard rate applied to private school fees from 1 January 2025 (Full Fact, 28 May 2026).

evidence.text: VAT at the standard rate of 20% has applied to private school fees since 1 January 2025.

probes.question: What did Labour’s manifesto promise on defence spending?

options.A: To set out the path to spending 2.5% of GDP on defence
options.B: To cut defence spending to 2% of GDP

probes.why: Manifesto, Strong foundations (pages 14 to 22): it will set out the path to spending 2.5% of GDP on defence. The government set 2.5% from April 2027 in February 2025.

evidence.text: we will set out the path to spending 2.5 per cent of GDP on defence.

probes.question: How many net additional homes does the government estimate were added in England from 9 July 2024 to 20 September 2026, against the 1.5 million target?

options.B: About 1.5 million, so the target is met

probes.why: GOV.UK housing supply indicators, April to June 2026: 437,900 estimated net additional homes, 29% of 1.5 million. The 208,600 figure is the official count for 2024-25 only.

evidence.text: The government estimates 437,900 net additional homes in England between 9 July 2024 and 20 September 2026: 29% of the 1.5 million target.

probes.question: In August 2026, what share of waiting pathways for consultant-led NHS treatment had waited up to 18 weeks?
probes.why: NHS England, RTT statistics for August 2026, published 8 October 2026: 65.2% within 18 weeks, against the 92% standard.

evidence.text: In August 2026, 65.2% of the 7.4 million waiting pathways for consultant-led treatment had waited up to 18 weeks.

questions.asked: how much harder is it to buy a house now than it was in the past
questions.reading: Read as how much the cost of buying a home has risen compared with earnings and with household budgets, over the longest series the site can check. Measured here: house prices against earnings from 1997 (England and Wales), a 10% deposit as years of median full-time pay before tax, average mortgage payments for owners with a mortgage in England after inflation (2008-09 to 2024-25), the average age of recent first-time buyers (2003-04 to 2024-25), home ownership by age (2008-09 to 2021-22), mortgage payments as a share of gross household income (2010-11 to 2024-25), and the average rate on new mortgages (January 2016 to September 2026). Not yet measured on the site: take-home pay (the mortgage share is before tax), mortgage payments before 2010-11 as a share of income, mortgage rates before 2016, and home ownership by age before 2008-09. Those stay open probes until the sources are added.

probes.question: Measured as years of pay before tax, how did the middle-priced home in England and Wales change between 1999 and the year to September 2025?

options.B: It stayed about the same
options.C: It rose by about a quarter

probes.why: Housing: house prices page. The middle-priced home cost 3.89 times median full-time earnings in 1999 and 7.55 times in the year to September 2025, so it nearly doubled.

evidence.text: cost 7.55 times
against 3.89 times in 1999

probes.question: In the year to September 2025, how many years of median full-time pay before tax would a 10% deposit on the middle-priced home come to?

options.B: About 0.8 years

probes.why: House prices page: a 10% deposit on the middle-priced home was £29,500 in the year to September 2025, which is 0.76 years of median full-time pay before tax (£7,000 and 0.39 years in 1999).

evidence.text: a 10% deposit on the middle-priced home was £29,500, which is 0.76 years

probes.question: After inflation, how did the average mortgage payment for owners with a mortgage in England change between 2008-09 and 2024-25?

options.A: It fell by about a fifth
options.B: It stayed about the same
options.D: It rose by more than half

probes.why: House prices page: after inflation, in 2024-25 prices, the average mortgage payment rose from £224 a week in 2008-09 to £242 a week in 2024-25, an increase of 8%.

evidence.text: rose from £224 a week in 2008-09 to £242 a week in 2024-25
an increase of 8%

probes.question: Do the mortgage payment figures show what someone buying a home today would pay each week?

options.B: No: they are for loans already taken out, at different times and rates

probes.why: House prices page: mortgage payments are for loans already taken out, at different times and rates, so they do not show what a new buyer pays.

evidence.text: so they do not show what a new buyer pays

probes.question: At what age do people today buy their first home, compared with earlier years?

options.B: About 31 in 2003-04 and about 34 in 2024-25, a rise of about three years

probes.why: House prices page: the average age of first-time buyers in England was 31 in 2003-04 and 34 in 2024-25 (English Housing Survey, Annex Table 3.3). The site shows recent first-time buyers, so the figures are averages and small samples.

evidence.text: rose from 31 in 2003-04 to 34 in 2024-25

probes.question: How has home ownership changed for people of each age since the 1990s?
probes.gap: The site shows home ownership by age from 2008-09 to 2021-22 (see J11.9), but not back to the 1990s: the earlier rows in the same source are not yet documented well enough to compare.

probes.question: What share of take-home pay goes on a mortgage payment for households with a mortgage, now and in 2008-09?
probes.gap: The site shows mortgage payments as a share of gross household income from 2010-11 (see J11.10). It cannot show take-home pay, which is not in the source, or 2008-09, which the table does not give.

probes.question: How have mortgage interest rates changed since 2008?
probes.gap: The site shows the average rate on new mortgages from January 2016 (see J11.11). It has no mortgage rate series back to 2008 yet.

probes.question: Between 2008-09 and 2021-22, how did home ownership change for people aged 25 to 34, and for people aged 75 and over?

options.A: It rose for both age groups
options.B: It fell for people aged 25 to 34 and rose for people aged 75 and over
options.C: It fell for both age groups
options.D: It stayed about the same for both age groups

probes.why: House prices page: the share of people aged 25 to 34 who owned their home fell from 51% in 2008-09 to 41% in 2021-22; for people aged 75 and over it rose from 72% to 80%. English Housing Survey live table FC2101.

evidence.text: fell from 51% to 41%
For people aged 75 and over it rose, from 72% to 80%

probes.question: What share of household income, before tax, goes on mortgage payments for owner occupiers who make them, in 2010-11 and in 2024-25?

options.A: About a tenth in both years
options.B: Close to a fifth in both years, and a little higher in 2024-25

probes.why: House prices page: the payment took 18% of gross household income in 2010-11 and 19% in 2024-25 (English Housing Survey, Annex Table 2.5). Income is gross, before tax, so it is not take-home pay.

evidence.text: took 18% of gross household income in 2010-11 and 19% in 2024-25

probes.question: Between January 2016 and September 2026, how did the average rate on new mortgages change?

options.A: It fell, from about 4.6% to about 2.5%
options.B: It rose by about two percentage points, from about 2.5% to about 4.6%
options.C: It stayed about the same, near 3%

probes.why: House prices page: the average rate on new mortgages rose from 2.47% in January 2016 to 4.63% in September 2026, peaking at 5.34% in November 2023 (Bank of England series CFMZ6JM).

evidence.text: rose from 2.47% in January 2016 to 4.63% in September 2026

questions.asked: How does UK productivity compare to other countries
questions.source: John, project chat, 2026-11-04 (question 9 of a list of ten)
questions.reading: Productivity is read as output per hour worked (GDP divided by hours worked), the standard international measure, with output per worker as a second measure. Other countries are read as the G7 (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK and the United States), because the ONS comparison covers them. Levels are in pounds converted with purchasing power parities; trends are after inflation and start in 2008. The series ends in 2021, when the ONS stopped publishing it, so the site says so rather than using later figures from another source.

probes.question: In 2021, how did UK output per hour worked compare with France and the United States?

options.B: Lower than both
options.C: Higher than France but lower than the United States

probes.why: Productivity page, 2021: UK £46.92 an hour, against £55.50 in France and £58.88 in the United States (in pounds at current prices, converted with purchasing power parities).

evidence.text: UK output per hour worked was £46.92
£58.88 in the United States
£55.50 in France

probes.question: From 2008 to 2021, after inflation, did UK output per hour worked rise more or less than the average of the other five G7 countries on the page?

options.B: Less

probes.why: Productivity page: UK output per hour rose by 3.9% between 2008 and 2021, while the other five G7 countries rose by 10.3% on average.

evidence.text: Over 2008 to 2021, UK output per hour rose by 3.9%
the other five G7 countries on this page rose by 10.3% on average

probes.question: What is the latest year of figures for this comparison, and why does the page stop there?

options.B: 2023; the figures are still being collected
options.C: 2021; the ONS stopped publishing the series in 2024
options.D: 2019; the figures before the pandemic are the only reliable ones

probes.why: Productivity page limits: the series ends in 2021, and the ONS stopped publishing it in 2024.

evidence.text: The series ends in 2021. The ONS stopped publishing it in 2024.

questions.asked: How has welfare spending changed in the last 50 years
questions.reading: Welfare is read as social security: benefits and the State Pension, as the OBR measures it, from 1955-56 (the first year of the series) to 2021-22 (the last year the OBR measured). It is shown after inflation (2025-26 prices), per person, as a share of GDP and as a share of all public spending, and with and without pensions (from 1978-79, when the OBR first splits it). Splitting it into the State Pension, working-age benefits, disability benefits, housing benefit, tax credits and Universal Credit, and Child Benefit over the same years is a separate probe.

probes.question: Between 1955-56 and 2021-22, how did welfare spending (social security) change as a share of GDP?

options.A: It fell, from about 10% of GDP to about 5%
options.B: It more than doubled, from about 5% of GDP to about 11%
options.C: It stayed at about 5% of GDP throughout
options.D: It was about 20% of GDP in both years

probes.why: Welfare page: 5.0% of GDP in 1955-56, a peak of 12.4% in 2012-13, and 10.8% in 2021-22.

evidence.text: As a share of GDP it was 5.0% in 1955-56, peaked at 12.4% in 2012-13, and was 10.8% in 2021-22.

probes.question: After inflation, how did total welfare spending in 2021-22 compare with 1955-56?

options.B: About twice as much

probes.why: Welfare page: £31.7bn in 1955-56 and £307bn in 2021-22, both in 2025-26 prices (about 9.7 times as much).

evidence.text: was £31.7bn in 1955-56 and £307bn in 2021-22, both after inflation.

probes.question: In 2021-22, what share of social security spending went to pensioners?

options.B: About a third

probes.why: Welfare page, with and without pensions: pensioners received 54% of social security in 2021-22, against 59% in 1978-79.

evidence.text: Pensioners received 54% of social security in 2021-22, against 59% in 1978-79.

probes.question: After inflation, how much welfare spending was there per person in 2021-22?

options.B: About £4,600

probes.why: Welfare page: £4,583 per person in 2021-22, in 2025-26 prices, averaged over everyone in the population.

evidence.text: Per person, after inflation, it was £1,862 in 1978-79 and £4,583 in 2021-22.

probes.question: On the site, what does the 'without pensions' measure of welfare leave out?

options.A: The benefits paid to pensioners, such as the State Pension
options.B: Child Benefit

probes.why: Welfare page, 'What counts as welfare here': without pensions is the non-pensioner figure, which leaves out benefits paid to pensioners.

evidence.text: Without pensions means the non-pensioner figure: benefits paid to people who are not pensioners, such as those for children, people of working age and disabled people.

probes.question: In 2021-22, how much of DWP benefit spending went on the State Pension?

options.B: About a third (33%)

probes.why: DWP benefit expenditure tables, Spring Forecast 2026: in 2021-22 the State Pension was £104.7bn of £239.4bn, or 43.7%. The DWP tables cannot be joined into one split across 50 years, so the split is shown for 2021-22 only, with 1955-56 for the State Pension's share.

evidence.text: In 2021-22 the State Pension was 43.7% of DWP benefit spending: £104.7bn out of £239.4bn.

probes.question: In 2021-22, which of these took the largest share of DWP benefit spending after the State Pension: Universal Credit, housing benefit, disability and carers' benefits, tax credits or Child Benefit?

options.B: Tax credits

probes.why: Universal Credit was 17.0% of DWP benefit spending in 2021-22, ahead of disability and carers' benefits (12.2%), housing benefit (6.7%), Child Benefit (4.6%) and tax credits (4.3%).

evidence.text: Universal Credit was 17.0%, housing benefit (not Universal Credit) 6.7%, disability and carers' benefits 12.2%, tax credits 4.3% and Child Benefit 4.6%.

questions.asked: How many people, espeicalyl high earners, need to leave the UK before tax receipts are meaningfully damaged?
questions.reading: Read as: how many people, especially high earners, would have to leave before the Income Tax lost is large enough to count as meaningful. The site gives the arithmetic from HMRC's tax by income band (a stated number of leavers, each counted at their group's average tax, before any other change), yardsticks a reader can weigh (one per cent of receipts; the OBR's forecast errors), and the OBR's evidence on how high earners respond to tax rates. What counts as meaningful is a judgement, and the site does not make it.

probes.question: In 2023-24, how many taxpayers had total income of £1 million or more?

options.B: About 26,000

probes.why: HMRC's Survey of Personal Incomes, Table 3.3, 2023-24: 26 thousand taxpayers in the band of £1 million and over.

evidence.text: 26,000 taxpayers had total income of £1 million or more

probes.question: In 2023-24, what share of all Income Tax did taxpayers with total income of £1 million or more pay?

options.B: About 10%

probes.why: Table 3.3: £27.7 billion of the £274 billion total, which is 10.1%.

evidence.text: Together they paid £27.7bn of Income Tax, 10.1% of the total

probes.question: If 1,000 taxpayers with total income of £1 million or more left the UK and nothing else changed, roughly how much Income Tax would be lost?

options.B: About £1.1 billion

probes.why: Their average Income Tax is about £1.07 million each, so 1,000 of them pay about £1.1 billion.

evidence.text: 1,000 leavers from this group would take £1.1bn of tax with them

probes.question: Does the site say exactly how many leavers would meaningfully damage receipts?

options.B: Yes: 100,000 leavers
options.C: No: it says that is a judgement and gives yardsticks instead
options.D: No: it says the question cannot be answered at all

probes.why: The page says the site does not set a threshold and that whether a loss is meaningful is a judgement, so it gives yardsticks rather than a verdict.

evidence.text: so the page gives yardsticks rather than a verdict
The site does not set a threshold

probes.question: One per cent of public sector receipts in 2023-24 is roughly the tax of how many taxpayers with total income of £1 million or more?

options.B: About 10,000

probes.why: One per cent of receipts is £11.0 billion, which is the tax of about 10,000 of the £1 million group (40% of it).

evidence.text: That is the tax of about 10,000 leavers from the £1 million group (40% of it)

probes.question: After HMRC's analysis of how high earners responded, what did the OBR say the underlying yield of the 50p rate was for 2012-13?

options.B: Reduced from £2.6 billion to £0.6 billion

probes.why: The OBR's 2014 review of the 50p rate says the estimated underlying yield for 2012-13 was reduced from £2.6 billion to £0.6 billion.

evidence.text: was also reduced from £2.6 billion to £0.6 billion

probes.question: What did the OBR's 2012 costing of the 50p rate say high earners might do in response?

options.A: Nothing: the rate had no effect
options.B: Work less, retire early, leave the country or use tax planning

probes.why: The OBR listed labour supply responses such as working less, retiring early or leaving the country, and greater tax planning, avoidance and evasion.

evidence.text: retiring early, or leaving the country

probes.question: By how much were 2024-25 receipts higher than the OBR's March 2023 forecast made two years before?

options.B: £35 billion

probes.why: The OBR's June 2026 evaluation says 2024-25 receipts were £35 billion (3.2%) higher than its March 2023 two-year-ahead forecast.

evidence.text: were £35 billion (3.2%) higher than its March 2023 forecast
